title: Skin Grafting
body:
## What it is
A skin graft is healthy skin placed over a burn or wound that cannot heal on its own. It closes the wound, reduces infection, fluid loss, heat loss and scarring. Closure is usually done between about the 5th and 21st day depending on the burn.

## Must-know facts
- Autograft: the client's own skin; permanent. Taken from a donor site; the graft is immobilised for about 3 to 7 days so it can attach.
- Allograft (homograft): donor skin from another human, often cadaver skin taken within 24 hours of death; temporary cover; rejection can occur within about 24 hours.
- Xenograft (heterograft): animal skin, often pig; temporary; replaced every 2 to 5 days until the wound heals or an autograft is done; rejection within about 24 to 72 hours.
- Synthetic or biosynthetic skin substitutes and cultured skin exist; some are transparent so the wound can be seen.
- Split-thickness graft: top layers; donor site heals itself in about 7 to 14 days; may be meshed to cover a larger area. Full-thickness graft: all layers; better look for face and hands, but the donor site must be closed.
- Graft needs a clean, well-supplied bed to take; fluid, blood or infection under it can lift it off. Bleeding beneath an autograft stops it from sticking.
- First dressing change usually 2 to 5 days after surgery, earlier if there is pus or a foul odour ([[Burn Wound Closure: Autograft, Allograft and Xenograft]]).

## What the nurse assesses
- Graft colour, adherence, drainage, odour, signs of infection or bleeding, donor site pain and bleeding, circulation, nutrition.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: a graft lives on blood supply from the bed, so anything that lifts or squeezes it (fluid, blood, movement, pressure, infection) kills it. So protect, immobilise and watch the bed.
- Safety: avoid shearing and pressure; keep the area elevated and still.
- Temporary covers buy time until an autograft can be done; only an autograft is permanent.
- Donor site: a partial-thickness wound that is painful; treat pain and keep dressing as ordered.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Immobilise and protect the graft site as ordered, avoiding pressure, shearing and moisture.
2. Elevate the area and avoid movement until the surgeon allows.
3. Keep dressing intact; observe for fluid collection; follow the order for first dressing change.
4. Care for the donor site (keep dry or covered as ordered); it is often more painful than the graft.
5. Prevent infection; encourage protein-rich nutrition.
6. Teach about sun protection, moisturising, scar care.

## How the exam asks about it
Which graft is temporary (allograft, xenograft, synthetic); which is permanent (autograft); what to do first when a graft looks blue or has blood collecting under it (report promptly); why a client with a new graft cannot have hydrotherapy. Trap: calling a xenograft permanent because it is a "graft".

## Related topics
[[Burn Wound Care Methods, Hydrotherapy and Debridement]], [[Phases of Burn Care]], [[Degrees of Burns]]

## Check against your textbook
- Exact timing of first dressing change, donor site dressing practice, and positioning rules.
- Handout times for rejection and immobilisation vary by source.

title: Antimicrobials for Burns
body:
## What it is
Topical antimicrobials are applied directly to burn wounds to prevent or treat infection. Systemic antibiotics are used for confirmed infection and not routinely as prevention.

## Must-know facts
- Silver sulfadiazine (Silvadene) cream: widely used, soothing, minimal penetration of eschar; used with open, light or occlusive dressings; applied one to three times daily after cleansing. Cautions: sulfa allergy (rash, itching, burning), temporary drop in white cells that clears in a few days, and a pseudo-eschar that is removed easily after about 72 hours and makes inspection harder. Store away from heat.
- Mafenide acetate (Sulfamylon) 5 to 10 percent cream: penetrates eschar, so used on deep burns, ears and cartilage and is the agent of choice for electrical burns in the handout. Cautions: painful during and after application (give analgesic about 30 minutes before) and metabolic acidosis; not used over large areas (the handout says not over 20 percent TBSA). Daily baths remove old cream.
- Silver nitrate 0.5 percent solution: bacteriostatic and fungicidal; does not penetrate eschar; dressings are kept wet, remoistened about every 2 hours; stains skin, linen and utensils grey or black; monitor sodium and potassium (can lower them).
- Others: cerium nitrate, povidone iodine, gentamicin (watch hearing, balance and kidneys), polymyxin B, bacitracin ointment (face and superficial wounds), silver-impregnated dressings.
- Nurses observe application technique: thin layer with sterile gloves, remove old product at each change, check sensitivities and report allergy.
- Tetanus prophylaxis should be checked.
- Culture the wound when infection is suspected before changing therapy.

## What the nurse assesses
- Allergy history, wound signs, temperature, white cell and acid-base results as ordered, pain on application, sodium and potassium with silver nitrate.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: each agent has a signature adverse effect, and the exam picks the agent from it: sulfa allergy and low white cells (silver sulfadiazine); pain and acidosis (mafenide); stains and electrolyte loss (silver nitrate).
- Safety: check allergy before the first application; sulfa allergy rules out both sulfa-based agents.
- Assess before acting: look at the wound and labs; treat pain first for painful agents.
- A dry crust-like layer after silver sulfadiazine is not always eschar; do not confuse it with wound worsening.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Check allergy and order before applying.
2. Use sterile technique and appropriate coverage.
3. Premedicate for painful agents.
4. Monitor laboratory findings and report abnormal ones.
5. Document and report infection signs.

## How the exam asks about it
Which agent is contraindicated in sulfa allergy; which causes acidosis; which stains; which penetrates eschar (mafenide); which does not (silver nitrate, silver sulfadiazine minimal). Pick the agent by its signature adverse effect.

## Related topics
[[Burn Wound Care Methods, Hydrotherapy and Debridement]], [[Pain, Infection and Nutrition in Burns]], [[Topical Antimicrobial Agents for Burns]], [[Sulfonamides and Urinary Anti-Infectives]]

## Check against your textbook
- Drug lists, concentrations, frequency and which agent your exam source prefers for which area; verify against pharmacology references.
- The handout calls silver sulfadiazine "most bactericidal"; confirm. The 20 percent TBSA limit for mafenide is doubtful.

title: Disaster Nursing Basic Concepts
body:
## What it is
A disaster is a sudden event that overwhelms the ability of a community to cope using its own resources and needs outside help. Disaster nursing applies nursing knowledge to protect health, give care and support recovery before, during and after such events. A common definition: a serious disruption of how a society functions, with widespread human, material or environmental losses beyond its own coping ability.

## Must-know facts
- Types: natural (typhoon, flood, earthquake, volcanic eruption, landslide), human-made (fire, transport accident, conflict, industrial or chemical accident, terrorism), and mixed. Mass casualty incident means many casualties at once; it may or may not be a disaster depending on local capacity.
- Hazard is the source of danger; vulnerability is how exposed and unprepared people are; capacity is what helps them cope; risk comes from hazard combined with vulnerability and low capacity. Disasters hurt most where vulnerability is high.
- Major risk groups: natural, technological (chemical, radiological), epidemics, and societal risks (poverty, exclusion, violence).
- Most vulnerable people: children, older adults, pregnant women, people with disability, chronic illness, poverty.
- Emergency means something needing immediate response; the main objective of emergency management is to decrease death, illness and disability.
- General principles (handout): first priority is protecting people at risk; second is protecting critical resources and systems; capabilities must be built before impact; management relies on understanding hazards and on teamwork across disciplines ([[Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Program]]).
- Disaster care differs from daily care: goal shifts to the greatest good for the greatest number, with limited resources, which is why disaster triage is used ([[NATO Disaster Triage System]]).
- Nurses' roles: preparedness teaching, triage, first aid, shelter and evacuation-centre care, infection and sanitation control, vaccination and surveillance, psychosocial support, record keeping, advocacy.
- Common health issues afterwards: injuries, infection outbreaks from poor water and sanitation, malnutrition, mental stress, interrupted care for chronic disease.
- Philippine legal roots: Presidential Decree 1566 (1978) on disaster control and community preparedness, the Local Government Code (RA 7160, which moved responsibilities to local units), and RA 10121 (2010) ([[NDRRMC and the Philippine Disaster Framework]]).

## What the nurse assesses
- Scene safety, number and condition of casualties, available resources, water and sanitation, vulnerable people, psychological state.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: overwhelmed local resources -> many casualties of mixed severity -> sort first, treat the savable first.
- Maslow and safety: your own safety, then life-saving care, then shelter, food, water and sanitation, then comfort and psychosocial care.
- Assess before acting: a rapid scene and casualty assessment decides what help to call.
- Prevent the second wave: outbreaks from contaminated water kill after the event, so sanitation and surveillance are priorities.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Personal and team safety first.
2. Rapid assessment and triage.
3. Life-saving care before comfort care.
4. Preventing secondary problems such as outbreaks.
5. Psychosocial support ([[Crisis and Crisis Intervention|Crisis Intervention]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Which role fits which phase, who is seen first in a mass casualty event, which action first at arrival to the scene (safety). Trap: confusing hazard with vulnerability, or choosing comfort care before life-saving care.

## Related topics
[[Disaster Management Continuum]], [[NATO Disaster Triage System]], [[NDRRMC and the Philippine Disaster Framework]], [[Crisis Types, Phases and Intervention Styles]]

## Check against your textbook
- Definitions differ between sources; use your reviewer's wording for exam definitions.
- Decree and law numbers come from the handout and from memory; confirm.

title: Disaster Management Continuum
body:
## What it is
The disaster management continuum (cycle) shows that disaster work is continuous, not just the response. Phases flow into one another: mitigation and prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery with rehabilitation. Many books group them as before, during and after.

## Must-know facts
- Prevention and mitigation: reduce the damage before disaster by stopping hazards or lowering risk. Examples: land-use planning, building codes, flood control, hazard mapping, community education.
- Preparedness: be ready to act. Examples: emergency plans, drills, early warning, stockpiling, trained volunteers, evacuation routes, family kits, community health assessment.
- Response: actions during and immediately after impact. Examples: search and rescue, triage, emergency treatment, evacuation, shelter, emergency food and water, disease control.
- Recovery and rehabilitation: return to normal or better. Examples: rebuilding, restoring services, counselling, follow-up of injured, lessons learned, updating plans.
- Nursing roles per phase: educate and train (before), triage and treat (during), long-term care and mental health follow-up (after).
- Philippine law frames the same ideas as four thematic areas ([[NDRRMC and the Philippine Disaster Framework]]).
- Capabilities must be developed before a hazard strikes; this is why preparedness is called the nurse's most useful phase.
- Health emergency programs follow the same cycle at the community level ([[Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Program]]).

## What the nurse assesses
- Before: community risk and readiness. During: casualties, needs. After: unmet health needs, outbreaks, stress.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: ask "has the hazard struck yet?" If no, the activity is mitigation or preparedness; if it is happening or just happened, response; if the immediate danger is over, recovery.
- Mitigation changes the hazard or the risk (a dike, a building code); preparedness prepares people to react (a drill, a kit). If the activity makes the event smaller, it is mitigation; if it makes people ready, it is preparedness.
- Priority within response follows ABC and safety first; Maslow places food, water and shelter before education.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Match the action to the phase: teaching and drills before, triage and care during, follow-up after.
2. Keep records and report.
3. Evaluate and improve plans.

## How the exam asks about it
Give an activity and ask which phase it belongs to (for example a drill is preparedness; setting up a first aid station is response; building a seawall is mitigation; counselling survivors weeks later is recovery). Trap: confusing mitigation with preparedness.

## Memory aid
"Reduce, ready, respond, recover" (my own wording).

## Related topics
[[Disaster Nursing Basic Concepts]], [[NDRRMC and the Philippine Disaster Framework]], [[NATO Disaster Triage System]], [[Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Program]]

## Check against your textbook
- Number and names of phases differ between texts (three, four or five). No handout in your set covers this cycle in detail, so this note rests on standard textbook knowledge.

title: NATO Disaster Triage System
body:
## What it is
NATO triage is a disaster and military-style system that sorts many casualties into groups by urgency and survivability, so limited help goes where it saves the most lives. It uses priority categories, often shown by colour tags.

## Must-know facts
- Immediate (T1, usually red): life-threatening but treatable and likely to survive with quick care, such as airway obstruction, severe bleeding, shock, tension pneumothorax.
- Delayed (T2, usually yellow): serious injuries that can wait a short time without immediate death risk, such as stable fractures or burns not threatening airway.
- Minimal (T3, usually green): minor injuries, walking wounded; they can wait or help themselves.
- Expectant (T4, often blue or grey; some systems use black): injuries so severe that survival is unlikely given available resources, for example massive head injury or very large burns; they receive comfort care and are rechecked when resources allow.
- Dead (often black) in many systems.
- Colour and label details vary by country and by textbook. State what your reviewer teaches; I am confident of the immediate, delayed, minimal, expectant structure.
- Triage in disaster is repeated and done where the casualty is found and again at the treatment area.
- START (simple triage and rapid treatment), a widely taught method, goes in this order: can the person walk (green)? If not, is breathing present (open airway; none = black/expectant)? Breathing rate above 30 a minute = immediate; then perfusion (no radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds = immediate); then mental status (cannot follow simple commands = immediate); otherwise delayed. Verify steps.
- Do not stop to treat in the field during first-pass sorting, except to open an airway or control bleeding quickly.
- Large burns: very extensive burns in a disaster may be placed expectant if resources are scarce, while smaller burns are delayed or immediate by airway involvement.
- Children and older adults may need a different yardstick; use pediatric tools where available.

## What the nurse assesses
- Ability to walk, breathing, circulation (pulse, capillary refill), ability to follow commands.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: resources are scarce, so the aim shifts from "sickest first" to "greatest number saved". The immediate group (savable with quick care) goes first.
- ABC still decides within the group: airway and bleeding problems are fixed fast because they are quick to fix and deadly.
- Walking wounded are green because walking proves airway, breathing and enough circulation.
- Reassess: a delayed casualty who worsens is retagged immediate; an expectant casualty with new resources may be reconsidered.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Sort quickly; identify the immediate group first.
2. Tag, move to the right zone, treat in category order.
3. Reassess regularly and retag.
4. Document.

## How the exam asks about it
Which category for a client with a given description; which casualty to treat first (immediate); what to do for the expectant group (comfort, reassess). Trap: assuming the most seriously injured always goes first; in disaster those unlikely to survive wait. Another trap: stopping to treat one casualty during the first sweep.

## Related topics
[[Triage Basics and Three-Level Triage]], [[Disaster Management Continuum]], [[Disaster Nursing Basic Concepts]], [[PENA Triage]]

## Check against your textbook
- Category numbers, colours (especially for expectant), and whether dead are a separate category.
- START cut-offs (breathing rate 30, capillary refill 2 seconds); no handout in your set covers triage, so this rests on standard textbook knowledge.

title: NDRRMC and the Philippine Disaster Framework
body:
## What it is
NDRRMC is the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, the Philippine body that leads national disaster risk reduction and response coordination. It operates under the law on Philippine disaster risk reduction and management passed in 2010 (Republic Act 10121), which replaced the older disaster coordinating council system.

## Must-know facts
- The law shifted the national approach from mainly responding after disasters to reducing risk beforehand, with community participation.
- The framework is organised around four thematic areas: disaster prevention and mitigation, disaster preparedness, disaster response, and disaster rehabilitation and recovery.
- The system works through councils at national, regional, provincial, city or municipal, and barangay levels. Local governments have a first-responder role (consistent with the Local Government Code, RA 7160, which gave local units more responsibility). The Office of Civil Defense supports the national council as its secretariat. Different government agencies lead the different areas (for example health, social welfare, public works, defence).
- Earlier law: Presidential Decree 1566 (1978) strengthened disaster control capability and set up a national program on community disaster preparedness ([[Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Program]]).
- Local disaster funds exist; details are for your textbook.
- The Department of Health runs health emergency management and coordinates health responders; nurses may be part of rapid response teams and evacuation centre care.
- All details here are general and may have been amended; verify local policy.

## What the nurse assesses
- Community hazards and readiness, evacuation centre conditions, health needs of evacuees, reporting channels.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: disaster hits a barangay first, so the barangay level is the first line; higher levels step in when local capacity is exceeded.
- Match the activity to the thematic area, using the same logic as the continuum: reduce hazard = prevention and mitigation; readiness = preparedness; act now = response; rebuild = rehabilitation and recovery ([[Disaster Management Continuum]]).
- Safety and Maslow: evacuation centres must provide safe water, sanitation, food, shelter and protection for vulnerable people before programs.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Know the local plan and who to report to.
2. Join drills and teach families about preparedness.
3. Respond within your role and report health data to authorities.

## How the exam asks about it
Name the council, the law, the four thematic areas, or which phase an activity belongs to. Trap: mixing the levels (barangay is the lowest and first line), or mixing the 2010 law with the older decree.

## Related topics
[[Disaster Management Continuum]], [[Disaster Nursing Basic Concepts]], [[NATO Disaster Triage System]], [[Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Program]]

## Check against your textbook
- Verify local policy: council membership and chair, agency roles, law amendments, exact wording of the four areas and DOH health emergency arrangements.
- Law numbers are from memory and the community health handout; confirm.

title: Cardiac Arrest and Basic Life Support Principles
body:
## What it is
Cardiac arrest is sudden loss of effective heart pumping, so the client is unresponsive, not breathing normally and has no pulse. Basic life support (BLS) keeps blood and oxygen flowing until the heart can be restarted.

## Must-know facts
- Rhythms: shockable (ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia) need defibrillation. Non-shockable (asystole, pulseless electrical activity) need high-quality compressions, airway support, medicines and treatment of the cause ([[ECG Waves and Intervals]]).
- Chain of survival: early recognition and call for help, early CPR, early defibrillation, advanced care, post-arrest care.
- Principles of good CPR: start promptly, push hard and fast on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone), allow full recoil, keep interruptions very short, avoid over-ventilation, rotate compressors when tired. Commonly taught adult figures: a rate of 100 to 120 a minute, depth about 5 to 6 cm, and 30 compressions to 2 breaths for one rescuer. Exact numbers change between guideline updates and age groups: verify against current guidelines.
- Use an automated external defibrillator as soon as available; follow its prompts; stand clear before a shock; resume compressions right after the shock.
- Reversible causes are searched for (often grouped as the Hs and Ts such as low oxygen, low volume, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, clots).
- Check for a pulse for no longer than the guideline time (about 10 seconds); if unsure, begin compressions. Carotid pulse in adults, brachial in infants, femoral during shock or arrest.
- Epinephrine is the emergency drug used in arrest and anaphylaxis ([[Adrenergic Agonists: Epinephrine, Dopamine and Related Drugs]]).
- Do-not-resuscitate orders and living wills are honoured when valid ([[Advance Directives]]); without a valid order, resuscitate.
- After return of circulation: airway, oxygen, monitoring, 12-lead ECG, temperature care and transfer to intensive care.

## What the nurse assesses
- Responsiveness, breathing, pulse, rhythm on monitor, scene safety.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: no pulse means no oxygen reaching the brain, so brain injury starts within minutes; compressions restore some flow, defibrillation restores a rhythm. Early compressions and early shock are the two things that change survival.
- Why compressions first in an adult: the blood still holds oxygen for the first minutes, and what is missing is the pump (ABC becomes CAB in cardiac arrest). For drowning, children and obvious breathing causes, ventilation matters more.
- Safety: scene safe, standard precautions, dry the chest and remove oxygen sources before shocking.
- Assess before intervening, but never delay compressions for tests or equipment.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Check safety and responsiveness, call for help and the defibrillator.
2. Start compressions (circulation first in adults).
3. Open the airway and ventilate as trained.
4. Defibrillate when a shockable rhythm is present.
5. Continue until relieved, the client recovers, or a valid order to stop; document the event.

## How the exam asks about it
Which action first (check response and call for help, then compressions). Which rhythm gets a shock. Trap: delaying compressions to find a pulse for too long or to intubate. Another: giving a shock for asystole.

## Related topics
[[Airway Obstruction and Choking]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]], [[ICU Monitoring Concepts]], [[Primary vs Secondary Survey]]

## Check against your textbook
- All numbers (rate, depth, ratio, shock energy, drug doses) and the sequence for children and infants. No handout in your set covers resuscitation, so this rests on standard textbook knowledge.

title: Airway Obstruction and Choking
body:
## What it is
Choking happens when a foreign body blocks the airway, either partly or fully. A full blockage is a life-threatening emergency within minutes.

## Must-know facts
- Mild (partial) obstruction: the person can cough, speak or breathe with noise. Encourage coughing; do not slap the back or perform thrusts while air still moves.
- Severe obstruction: cannot speak, cough or breathe; may clutch the throat (universal choking sign), have silent struggle, turn blue.
- Conscious adult or child: abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre) repeatedly until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive. Pregnant or very obese clients: chest thrusts instead.
- Infant: alternating back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts; never blind finger sweeps. Exact numbers per cycle (commonly five of each): verify against current guidelines.
- If the person becomes unresponsive: lower to the ground, call for help, and begin CPR; look in the mouth before ventilating and remove an object only if you can see it ([[Cardiac Arrest and Basic Life Support Principles]]).
- Hospital: trained providers may use suction, forceps or advanced airway or surgical airway.
- Choking in an unconscious client who is breathing noisily with snoring is usually the tongue, not a foreign body: open the airway first ([[Airway Management in the Primary Survey]]).
- After thrusts, the person should be checked by a provider because abdominal thrusts can injure organs.
- Prevention: cut food small, supervise children, avoid small objects and some foods for young children (nuts, hard sweets, whole grapes), careful eating for people with swallowing difficulty; the chewing and swallowing risk rises with dementia, stroke and sedation.

## What the nurse assesses
- Ability to cough and speak, colour, breathing effort, level of consciousness.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: a solid object blocks air -> cannot speak or cough -> if air still moves, let the body clear it (least invasive first); if no air moves, force pressure to expel it (thrusts) at once.
- Why not thrust a coughing client: a thrust may move a partial blockage into a full one.
- Why back blows plus chest thrusts in infants: abdominal thrusts can damage a baby's liver; their small size lets back blows work.
- Maslow and ABC: this is an airway emergency; nothing outranks it.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Ask "Are you choking?" and check if the person can speak or cough.
2. If severe, call for help and begin thrusts right away.
3. If the person collapses, start CPR.
4. After recovery, assess and have the person medically checked.

## How the exam asks about it
Which action first when a client can cough (encourage coughing, observe). Which technique for infants (back blows plus chest thrusts). Trap: doing abdominal thrusts on an infant, or sweeping the mouth blindly.

## Related topics
[[Airway Management in the Primary Survey]], [[Cardiac Arrest and Basic Life Support Principles]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]]

## Check against your textbook
- Number of thrusts and blows and the sequence by age; verify against current guidelines. No handout in your set covers choking, so this rests on standard textbook knowledge.

title: Respiratory Failure Recognition
body:
## What it is
Respiratory failure means the lungs cannot keep blood oxygen or carbon dioxide at safe levels. It may develop fast (acute) or on top of chronic lung disease.

## Must-know facts
- Hypoxaemic (type 1) failure: low oxygen with normal or low carbon dioxide, for example pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, acute respiratory distress syndrome, pulmonary embolism ([[Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)]], [[Pulmonary Embolism]]). In ARDS the low oxygen does not improve with extra oxygen; it develops over about 4 to 48 hours with severe breathlessness and bilateral lung shadows on X-ray, and is treated with ventilation and positive end-expiratory pressure.
- Hypercapnic (type 2) failure: high carbon dioxide from poor ventilation, for example advanced COPD, drug overdose, neuromuscular weakness, chest wall injury, exhaustion.
- Early signs: restlessness, anxiety, fast breathing, fast pulse, use of accessory muscles. Later signs: confusion, drowsiness, blue colour, slow tiring breathing, falling saturation. Drowsiness with high carbon dioxide is dangerous.
- Arterial blood gases confirm the picture. Normal: pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaO2 80 to 100 mm Hg, PaCO2 35 to 45 mm Hg, HCO3 22 to 26. Failure shows low PaO2, high PaCO2 and a falling pH (respiratory acidosis) in the late stage ([[Arterial Blood Gas Basics]], [[Respiratory Acidosis]]). Oxygen saturation normally 95 to 100 percent.
- Clients with long-term CO2 retention need cautious controlled oxygen, but oxygen must never be withheld from someone who is hypoxic.
- Treatment: treat the cause, oxygen (device chosen by need: cannula for low flow, non-rebreather for the highest concentration), positioning (upright), airway clearance, bronchodilators or other drugs as ordered, non-invasive ventilation or mechanical ventilation when needed ([[Oxygen Therapy: Safety and Delivery Devices]]).
- Common precipitants: pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, sedatives, opioids, spinal cord injury or neuromuscular disease (the diaphragm weakens), and severe asthma.
- Shock and respiratory failure often travel together; sepsis and burns can start both.

## What the nurse assesses
- Respiratory rate and pattern, effort, saturation, colour, mental status, breath sounds, blood gases, fatigue.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: poor gas exchange or poor ventilation -> low oxygen or high CO2 -> restlessness first, then drowsiness. The restless client is still compensating; the drowsy client with slow breathing is tiring.
- Maslow and ABC: oxygenation is the most urgent need; sitting upright and oxygen are the least invasive first steps; escalate to ventilation when tiring.
- Why not sedate an anxious breathless client: sedatives suppress breathing and mask the sign (restlessness) that tells you oxygen is falling.
- Unstable before stable: a slow, drowsy breather outranks a fast, anxious one who is still talking.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway and breathing; call for help early.
2. Sit the client upright, give oxygen as ordered.
3. Monitor continuously and report deterioration quickly.
4. Prepare for ventilation support and transfer to a higher level of care.
5. Reassure the client and reduce oxygen demand.

## How the exam asks about it
Spot the early sign (restlessness), not only the late ones (cyanosis). Which client first when comparing a calm one with a slow, drowsy breathing one. Which gas result shows ventilatory failure (high CO2, low pH). Trap: giving a sedative for anxiety.

## Related topics
[[Breathing Assessment in the Primary Survey]], [[ICU Monitoring Concepts]], [[Cardiac Arrest and Basic Life Support Principles]], [[Chest X-ray and Pulse Oximetry]]

## Check against your textbook
- Gas values, oxygen delivery targets for chronic lung disease, and ventilation settings.
- Normal values are from the fundamentals handout; type 1 and 2 labels are standard textbook usage.

title: Sepsis and Septic Shock Recognition
body:
## What it is
Sepsis is a life-threatening response to infection that injures the body's own organs. Septic shock is sepsis with dangerously low blood pressure and poor tissue perfusion that persists despite fluids. Both are time-critical.

## Must-know facts
- Sources: pneumonia, urinary tract, abdomen, wounds and burns, lines and catheters. Higher risk: older adults, infants, diabetes, immune suppression, recent surgery, invasive devices. In burns, sepsis is a leading cause of illness because skin protection is lost and immunity is depressed ([[Burn Pathophysiology and Whole-Body Response]]).
- Septic shock is a distributive shock: bacterial toxins (often gram-negative) make vessels leak plasma into tissue and dilate ([[Distributive Shock: Neurogenic, Anaphylactic and Septic]]).
- Early clues: fever or low temperature, fast pulse, fast breathing, confusion, warm flushed skin early, reduced urine output. Later: low blood pressure, cool mottled skin, high lactate.
- Quick bedside screens exist (such as qSOFA: fast breathing, altered mentation, low systolic pressure); verify criteria in your textbook.
- Early care principles (often called a bundle): recognise early, get blood cultures before antibiotics without delaying them, give broad-spectrum antibiotics early, give IV fluids, measure lactate, start vasopressors if pressure stays low, find and control the source (remove infected lines, drain abscesses). Exact timing, volumes and drug choices follow current guidelines ([[Vasopressors for Hypotension and Shock]]).
- Complications: shock, acute respiratory distress, kidney injury, DIC and multiple organ failure ([[DIC and Multiple Organ Dysfunction Recognition]]).
- Older adults and neonates may show confusion, poor feeding or low temperature rather than fever.
- Prevention is nursing work: hand hygiene, aseptic technique for lines and wounds, early removal of catheters, mouth care and early mobilisation.

## What the nurse assesses
- Temperature, pulse, breathing, blood pressure trend, mental status, skin, urine output, wound and line sites, laboratory results (white count, lactate, cultures).

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: infection triggers body-wide inflammation -> vessels dilate and leak -> pressure falls and organs starve. Because organ damage progresses by the hour, the first action is early recognition and escalation, then cultures and antibiotics, then fluids.
- Why cultures before antibiotics: antibiotics sterilise the sample, but never wait long for cultures if it delays treatment.
- Safety and infection control: strict hand hygiene protects the next client.
- Assess before intervening; least invasive first: fluids and antibiotics before vasopressors; ABC and oxygen throughout.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Recognise and escalate at once.
2. Airway, breathing, oxygen, IV access.
3. Collect cultures, then give antibiotics promptly as ordered.
4. Give fluids as ordered; monitor response and urine output.
5. Prevent spread: hand hygiene, remove unneeded lines as ordered.

## How the exam asks about it
Early subtle changes (new confusion in an older adult) as the first sign. Which order: cultures before antibiotics but do not delay antibiotics. Trap: waiting for fever. Another: identifying warm flushed skin as an early septic shock sign.

## Related topics
[[Types of Shock]], [[Management of Shock]], [[ICU Monitoring Concepts]], [[Burns: Causes and Overview]]

## Check against your textbook
- Definitions (these have changed over time), bundle timing, screening tools, fluid and drug details.

title: DIC and Multiple Organ Dysfunction Recognition
body:
## What it is
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is widespread, abnormal clotting that uses up clotting factors and platelets, so the client both clots and bleeds. Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) is failure of two or more organ systems, often after shock, sepsis, trauma or burns.

## Must-know facts
- DIC is always secondary to something: sepsis, major trauma, burns, obstetric emergencies (abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism, retained dead fetus; see [[Postpartum Hemorrhage]]), cancer, transfusion reactions ([[Blood Transfusion Reactions]]), snakebite.
- Signs of bleeding: oozing from IV sites, nosebleeds, gum bleeding, blood in urine or stool, bruises and tiny red spots, bleeding from wounds. Signs of clotting: cold blue fingers or toes, organ ischaemia, confusion, low urine output.
- Typical laboratory pattern: low platelets, prolonged clotting times, raised fibrin breakdown products (such as D-dimer) and low fibrinogen; verify values.
- Management focuses on treating the cause, supporting circulation, and replacing blood products as ordered. Avoid injections and rough handling where possible.
- MODS: kidney, lung, liver, heart, gut, brain and blood systems may fail one after another. Prevention is the main strategy: treat shock early, control infection, support nutrition, and monitor trends. Burn care teaches the same principle: "resuscitate", meaning immediate support for any failing organ system.
- Late irreversible shock leads to MODS: anuria, ARDS, liver and gut failure ([[Early vs Late Stages of Shock]], [[Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)]]).
- Blood is typed and cross-matched early; fresh frozen plasma, platelets and cryoprecipitate are the usual products; check each product with a second nurse ([[Blood Products and Preparing a Transfusion]]).

## What the nurse assesses
- Bleeding sites, skin and extremity colour, vital signs, urine output, mental status, laboratory trend, oxygen saturation.
- Measure blood loss: weigh pads, record drainage, measure abdominal girth or limb size if concealed bleeding is suspected.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: a trigger switches on clotting everywhere -> clotting factors and platelets are used up -> bleeding appears in unrelated places while small vessels block. So treat the trigger first, and protect the client from any extra bleeding.
- Why avoid injections and invasive procedures: every puncture is a new bleeding site; use pressure for longer than usual.
- Priority order: airway, breathing, circulation (stop and replace blood), then cause, then comfort.
- Early recognition: bleeding at several unrelated sites in a very sick client is DIC until proved otherwise; report at once.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Report early signs of bleeding or unexpected bruising in a sick client.
2. Protect from injury: gentle handling, soft toothbrush, pressure on puncture sites, avoid intramuscular injections.
3. Give blood products and drugs as ordered; monitor reactions.
4. Support each failing organ and monitor trends.

## How the exam asks about it
Which clients are at risk (sepsis, obstetric emergency, trauma). Which finding means DIC is developing (bleeding from several unrelated sites). Trap: treating the bleeding alone without the cause; choosing an intramuscular injection.

## Related topics
[[Sepsis and Septic Shock Recognition]], [[Early vs Late Stages of Shock]], [[ICU Monitoring Concepts]], [[Complete Blood Count and Reference Values]]

## Check against your textbook
- Lab reference values, product choice and heparin use in DIC (debated), and the MODS scoring systems. No handout in your set covers DIC, so this rests on standard textbook knowledge.

title: ICU Monitoring Concepts
body:
## What it is
Intensive care uses continuous monitoring and rapid action to catch deterioration early in acutely ill clients. The nurse interprets trends, responds to alarms and acts before the client collapses.

## Must-know facts
- Continuous ECG, pulse oximetry, and frequent blood pressure; arterial lines give beat-to-beat pressure and sample blood for gases. Zero and level the transducer as taught; damped waveforms need troubleshooting. Before an arterial puncture or line at the wrist, the Allen test checks that the ulnar artery supplies the hand (colour should return within about 6 seconds) ([[Arterial Blood Gases and Allen's Test]]).
- Pulse oximetry: normal is 95 percent or higher; sensor sites include fingertip, earlobe, forehead and toe ([[Chest X-ray and Pulse Oximetry]]). ECG monitoring reads rhythm ([[ECG Waves and Intervals]]).
- Arterial blood gas normals: pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaO2 80 to 100, PaCO2 35 to 45, HCO3 22 to 26 ([[Arterial Blood Gas Basics]]). Press the puncture site at least 5 minutes (15 minutes if on anticoagulants), and send the sample on ice.
- Central venous catheters give access for drugs and pressure measurement; risks include infection, air embolism and bleeding.
- Mean arterial pressure reflects organ perfusion; urine output (an hourly indwelling catheter measure; about 30 mL an hour or more in adults) is an easy bedside measure of kidney perfusion; mental status reflects brain perfusion.
- Mechanical ventilation: watch the alarms, secretions, tube position, sedation level, and comfort. Prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia with mouth care, head-of-bed elevation, hand hygiene and daily review of readiness to wean. Turn the client frequently, give nutrition (the ARDS handout suggests 35 to 45 kcal/kg/day) and rest to cut oxygen use.
- Neurological monitoring: GCS, pupils, intracranial pressure when a device is placed ([[Level of Consciousness and Glasgow Coma Scale]]).
- Sedation and delirium are assessed with scales; pain is assessed even in clients who cannot speak.
- Early warning scores combine vital signs into a trigger for escalation.
- Never silence or ignore an alarm without checking the client first.
- Emergency equipment (suction, oxygen, bag-valve-mask, defibrillator) is checked at the start of each shift.

## What the nurse assesses
- The client first, then the monitor. Trends over hours, not single numbers. Lines, tubes and drains each shift.

## How to reason about it
- Cause -> finding -> priority: a worrying number may mean the patient or the equipment; look at the client first (airway, breathing, circulation), then the probe, lead or line. Treat the client, not the monitor.
- Why trends matter: single readings vary with position, movement and probes; a steady drift in pulse, urine or mental state shows true deterioration.
- Safety: infection prevention for every device; secure tubes; keep alarms on and audible.
- Assess before intervening; escalate early with clear data (what changed, since when, what you did).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Look at the client before the monitor.
2. Check ABCs when an alarm sounds.
3. Escalate trends early.
4. Prevent device infections and pressure injuries; document.
5. Keep family informed and support them.

## How the exam asks about it
A monitor shows a worrying number but the client looks fine (check equipment, e.g. probe, then recheck the client). Or a client looks poor but numbers look acceptable (trust assessment). Another: the first action when a ventilator alarm sounds (assess the client, disconnect and bag if needed).

## Related topics
[[Respiratory Failure Recognition]], [[Management of Shock]], [[Disability and Exposure in the Primary Survey]], [[Sepsis and Septic Shock Recognition]]

## Check against your textbook
- Normal pressure ranges, ventilator settings and local ICU protocols.
